concepts.premise: Rank 1 of 12. Ch1 cold open + Ch6 payoff. Suggested Short title: "Every Photo of Hawaii Is Cropped". A postcard of a Big Island beach gets un-cropped: the paper border peels away, the ocean drains, and the beach turns out to be the top of a mountain so heavy it dented the planet. Delivers the film's thesis ("only the tip") in 28 s. Understandable with no context: everyone has seen a Hawaii beach photo.
concepts.hook: Line at 0.0 s: "Every photo of Hawaii is cropped." Frame 0: a paper cut-out postcard (a real PD photo of a Big Island beach on Mauna Loa's flank, e.g. NPS/USGS, VERIFY rights; fallback: our own render with a paper border) fills about 80% of the frame width, tilted 3 degrees. Big printed "HAWAII" across its top (Anton cap 170 px, y 330-500). The same coast is rendered in the engine behind it and lined up with the photo.
concepts.payoff: The counter climbs from the dented true base to the summit and lands on "56,000 FT" (the only number). "From that real base, Mauna Loa is about fifty-six thousand feet tall. Almost twice Everest." The Everest silhouette, on the same base line, reaches about halfway. This is the gasp. Spine facts #2/#3; the narration says "about" and "almost" and names Mauna Loa. Scheduling note: this spends the long-form's climax, so publish it about 7-10 days after the long-form with the long-form as Related Video. Swap the number to 33,500 FT (Mauna Kea, fact #1) only if the showrunner wants to protect the payoff.
concepts.loop: Read together: "Put the ocean back, and / every photo of Hawaii is cropped." The refill rushes up the flank, and the camera eases back up to the beach on the frame-0 keyframe. The paper border flips back in from all four edges (paper-flap SFX), so the last frame is the frame-0 postcard: same camera, same water level, same tilt. Record the last line and the first line as one Rodney take and split it at the seam so the intonation carries over. VO word 1 starts at frame 0. The last word ends 3 frames before the cut. Cut the music at a bar line. No end card.

concepts.reuses: The Ch1 0:00 thumbnail-in-motion camera and the HMRG + ETOPO Big Island terrain with the water plane and the SEA LEVEL line. The Ch3 drain to the floor and the Hawaiian Deep moat. concepts.why_watched_to_end: The first line is a provocation every viewer can test against their own memory of Hawaii photos. Each drain step raises the stakes: the beach, then the shore, then the slope, then "the floor isn't the bottom either". The number arrives at 19-23 s. The refill re-crops the picture right as the viewer works out what "cropped" meant, so the replay rewards them: they now see the postcard knowing what is under it. One big number and one continuous camera move, with nothing to skip past.
concepts.probe: There is no Hawaii-only drain Short. The adjacent premises are proven huge: "What If The Ocean Got Flushed?" 23M, "Hawaii Is Much Bigger Than You Think - The Secret Hidden Islands" 14M, "Can You Drain The Atlantic Ocean" 10M, "How Long Is Hawaii, Really?" 7.4M, "How Big is the Biggest Volcano?" 2.6M. The 56,000-ft true height is absent from Shorts: the closest is "The tallest volcano on Earth is Mauna Loa... 9,170" at 1.9K. "Hawaii drained ocean" returns only storm-drain surfing clips and a 28K "What If The Pacific Ocean Drained?". Our edge is a real-bathymetry drain past the sea floor, a number nobody uses, and a postcard device that makes the loop.

concepts.premise: Rank 2 of 12. Ch1 0:14-0:27 (Maui Nui at -400 ft plus the suitcase gag). Suggested title: "You Can't Walk From Maui to Lanai (Unless...)". A paper tourist with a suitcase wants to walk to the next island. We drain 400 ft of ocean, three islands fuse, and he strolls past a beached ferry. Twist: in the last Ice Age this was real. Then the sea comes back and he has to race the tide home.
concepts.hook: Line at 0.0 s: "You can't walk from Maui to Lanai." Frame 0: low oblique from the West Maui shore looking southwest. Lanai sits on the horizon in the top third, Molokai is at the upper left, and the channel is turquoise. A paper cut-out tourist (real PD traveller photo with a suitcase, NARA/LoC, VERIFY rights) stands at the waterline at centre-left with his feet at y about 1350 and a wave washing over his toes. Labels: "MAUI" by his feet and "LANAI" on the horizon island (Barlow cap 90).
concepts.payoff: The gag comes first: he hops across the dry channel floor past a paper ferry lying on its side on the seabed ("No ferry needed"). The real payoff follows: "And this isn't a what-if. In the last Ice Age, Maui, Molokai and Lanai really were one island." One number: "-400 FT". Spine fact #5 and must-fix #1: Kaho'olawe stays separate and dimmed, and the Penguin Bank lobe surfaces. VERIFY on the HMRG grid that the saddles really surface at -120 to -130 m.
concepts.loop: Read together: "Then the ice melted, the sea came back, and ever since, / you can't walk from Maui to Lanai." During the refill the tourist grabs his suitcase and races back ahead of the rising water. He lands on his frame-0 mark on the Maui shore as the wave reaches his toes. The camera eases onto the frame-0 keyframe and the -400 FT plate rolls back off. The last frame is frame 0. Record the last and first lines as one take and split it at the seam.

concepts.premise: Rank 3 of 12. Ch2 1:20-3:10 (Pali hat gag, Nu'uanu debris field, Manhattan overlay). Suggested title: "Half of This Volcano Is Missing". A tourist at Oahu's windy Pali Lookout loses his hat over the cliff. We follow it out to sea, drain the ocean, and find the other half of the volcano lying on the seafloor in giant blocks. One block is Manhattan-sized, and the hat is sitting on it.
concepts.hook: Line at 0.0 s: "Hold on to your hat." Frame 0: low oblique at the Nu'uanu Pali Lookout on the real Ko'olau terrain, with the stone railing in the foreground. A paper cut-out tourist (real PD photo of a man in a hat, VERIFY rights) stands at the railing with his jacket flapping. Green cliffs fall away to the windward coast, and the ocean fills the top third. Kicker "PALI LOOKOUT, OAHU" (Barlow cap 80, y 220). A wind-gust SFX plays at frame 0 and the hat is already lifting.
concepts.payoff: The blocks surface one after another, then a true-size Manhattan outline (6 px white outline, 55% orange fill) drops from the top of the frame and slams onto the largest block: "One of these pieces is the size of Manhattan." Then the crash zoom: the tiny hat is sitting on the Manhattan block. No big number on screen; the only spoken number is "more than a million years ago". Spine fact #6. VERIFY: measure the block on the HMRG/GLORIA data; if it is much larger, say "bigger than Manhattan" and let the overlay show it.
concepts.loop: Read together: "So next time you're up here, / hold on to your hat. About half of this volcano is missing." From the hat on the block, a 6-frame motion-blurred whip-pan runs back up the cliffs to the lookout. The tourist now wears a new hat and clamps it with both hands, and the wind ramps up. The shot settles on the exact frame-0 camera and pose. On the replay the gust lifts the new hat, so the loop doubles as a gag. Record it as one take and split at the seam.

concepts.premise: Rank 4 of 12. Ch3 3:30-4:40 (the Big Island stands up, Everest at the same scale, 33,500 ft, the climber vs the summit road). Suggested title: "The Highest Point on Earth Isn't on the Tallest Mountain". A paper climber plants his flag on Everest. Then we drain the ocean around Hawaii and Mauna Kea rises taller from its base, and someone drives up to near its top. The worn "taller than Everest" fact, retold as a rivalry with a punchline.
concepts.hook: Line at 0.0 s: "This is the highest point on Earth." Frame 0: the Everest summit ridge (SRTM 1", VE 1.0, low oblique) under a blue sky with spindrift. A paper cut-out climber (a real PD mountaineer photo, e.g. US Army 10th Mountain Division via NARA, VERIFY rights) plants a flag on the summit, and the flag is snapping. Label "EVEREST" (Barlow cap 110, y 260).
concepts.payoff: Live drain: Mauna Kea rises out of its full base beside Everest at the same scale. The "33,500 FT" counter rolls as the water falls, and a yellow dashed line at Everest's summit height shows Mauna Kea poking above it. "From the sea floor, Mauna Kea is more than thirty-three thousand feet tall. Taller than Everest." The laugh: a paper 4x4 (a PD vehicle photo) rolls up to the observatory domes and the driver steps out in shorts: "And you can drive almost to the top." Cut back to the climber's drooping flag ("Meanwhile, this guy..."). Spine facts #1 and #3. VERIFY #20 (the summit road). The wording "almost to the top" is already safe. Keep the gag respectful of Mauna Kea.
concepts.loop: Read together: "Put the ocean back, and once again, / this is the highest point on Earth." The refill sinks Mauna Kea back to "just an island". A whip-pan returns to Everest, the climber raises the drooping flag, it snaps in the wind, and the shot lands on the exact frame-0 camera and pose. The line is true both ways: sea level is Everest's home turf. Record it as one take and split at the seam.

concepts.probe: The most proven premise of the set, and the most spent: "Mount Everest is NOT the Tallest Mountain" 17M, "The real tallest mountain..." 15M, "Mount Everest is NOT the tallest mountain in the world" 2.1M, "Why This Mountain is TALLER than Mount Everest" 421K, "Mount Everest vs. Mauna Kea" 376K, plus 255K and 108K. Our edge: a true-scale live drain on real bathymetry instead of side-by-side bars, a two-character comedy, and a loop. The risk is fatigue with the fact, which is why it ranks 4 and not 1.

concepts.premise: Rank 5 of 12. Ch4 7:30-7:50 (French Frigate Shoals, the 2018 vanished island, the monk seal gag, La Perouse Pinnacle). Suggested title: "A Hurricane Washed Away This Seal's Island". A Hawaiian monk seal dozes on its sand island until a 2018 hurricane washes most of it away. Draining the water shows what the sand was sitting on: a whole sunken volcano, with one last rock left above the sea. Then the island grows back.
concepts.hook: Line at 0.0 s: "Islands out here can wash away in one storm." Frame 0: tight low shot of a paper cut-out Hawaiian monk seal (a real NOAA PD photo) dozing on white sand. Turquoise shallows sit behind it, and a dark storm band creeps in at the top of the frame. Kicker "FRENCH FRIGATE SHOALS" (Barlow cap 80, y 220).
concepts.payoff: Two turns. (1) The gag: the seal plops into the water as the sand streams off, surfaces, and looks left and right at an empty reef. (2) The gasp: the drain shows the reef standing on the shoulders of a huge drowned volcano, with La Perouse Pinnacle lit by the yellow rim: "A whole volcano, sunk out of sight. That rock is the last piece still above the sea." The happy ending: "The island is growing back. More than half of it has returned." Spine fact #10 (most of East Island eroded by Walaka in Oct 2018; about 60% back by 2024). No big number. Light VERIFY: monk seals haul out at French Frigate Shoals (NOAA).
concepts.loop: Read together: "The good news? It's growing back. But remember, / islands out here can wash away in one storm." After the regrowth time-lapse the seal flops back onto the new sand. The camera pushes back into the tight frame-0 shot: the seal dozing, the storm band edging into the top. The tight framing hides the island's outline, so the regrown 2024 shape matches the frame-0 sand exactly. Record it as one take and split at the seam.

concepts.premise: Rank 6 of 12. Ch4 5:45-8:00 plus Ch5 8:15 and 9:55 (hotspot candle, time-machine flight, Nihoa, La Perouse, Midway's ring, Kure's Darwin Point). Suggested title: "Every Hawaiian Island Ends Up Like This". It opens on the ending, empty ocean over a drowned volcano, then shows one Hawaiian island's whole life in 30 s: born on fire, carried northwest, worn down, reduced to a ring of coral, and drowned.
concepts.hook: Line at 0.0 s: "Every island in Hawaii ends up like this." Frame 0: the open Pacific at Kure's position, low oblique. The bright water plane is semi-transparent, so the dark flat-topped silhouette of a drowned volcano shows beneath it, and one seabird glides across. Kicker "EVERY HAWAIIAN ISLAND" (Barlow cap 80) over the headline "ENDS LIKE THIS" (Anton cap 150), y 220-470.
concepts.payoff: The life story ends at Midway: the "28 MILLION YEARS" counter (the only number) and a quick drain-and-slice showing the coral cap on the sunken volcano: "By about twenty-eight million years, the volcano has sunk out of sight. Only a ring of coral is left on top." Then the reveal that closes the circle: "Past here, coral can't keep up, and the volcano drowns for good." We are back at frame 0 and now know what we were looking at. Spine facts #8, #9, #10, #11 and #13. "About twenty-eight million" is the pedant wording. No morphing between islands; each real island is shown at its real position.
concepts.loop: Read together: "Past here, coral can't keep up, and the volcano drowns for good. / Every island in Hawaii ends up like this." At Kure the water rises over the reef ring and the ring fades under the surface. The camera settles on the frame-0 composition: the same drowned silhouette under bright water, the same seabird path, the age bar full. On the replay "like this" is no longer a mystery but a verdict. Record it as one take and split at the seam.

concepts.why_watched_to_end: It opens on an ending the viewer cannot read yet, so curiosity carries them through the story. Every 1.5-3 s there is a new island, a new stage of age, and a new shape (lava, green, canyons, sliver, tooth, ring). The number comes late, at 19 s, as the climax. The last line turns the first frame from an empty ocean into a grave, so the replay lands differently. This is the most "satisfying" structure of the set.

concepts.premise: Rank 7 of 12. Ch5 8:45-9:55 (the battle, the honest wreck geography, three hull silhouettes on the abyssal plain). Suggested title: "Where Are the Ships From the Battle of Midway?" A myth-buster with respect: the carriers are not at Midway. Drain the ocean and draw the line, and they lie far out on the flat ocean floor, about three miles down. Two have never been found. No gags; these are war graves.
concepts.hook: Line at 0.0 s: "Where are the carriers from the Battle of Midway?" Frame 0: Midway Atoll from a low oblique at golden hour, a calm sea, and the reef ring in the lower middle of the frame (above y 1500). Headline "MIDWAY" (Anton cap 150, y 300). Quiet low strings, with no sting.
concepts.payoff: "Not here." A thick yellow line (12 px core with a dark under-stroke) draws from the atoll far out across the drained abyssal plain. Then a vertical plunge down the water column (this format is built for depth) to three simple home-built hull silhouettes, with the "3 MILES DOWN" counter as the only number: "Three have been found, about three miles down. Two have never been found." Two empty dashed markers fade in and out. Spine facts #14 and #15 and must-fix #2: only the three surveyed wrecks, no positions implied for the unfound two, no OET/NOAA imagery, no treasure framing, music down. concepts.premise: Working title: 'We Pulled the Plug on Hawaii'. Someone yanks a giant bath plug next to Hawaii's Big Island. In one continuous live shot the ocean drains away while a vintage paper surfer rides the falling water down. The beach becomes a ledge, the ledge becomes a cliff, and five volcanoes merge into one mountain standing on the sea floor. Then the sea refills and the plug drops back in. Pure watch-it-happen satisfaction with one true payoff: the postcard island is only the tip. Producer rank #2 of 12. If S12 is also picked, S01 must stay on the northeast (Hilo / Mauna Kea) side with the surfer and plug so the two Big Island drains never look alike. Facts: spine #1 and #4. 'Five volcanoes' comes from the brief's 3:30 scene line (standard USGS) but is not in the spine table, so VERIFY the wording.

Turquoise sea fills the lower half; the green island and Mauna Kea's summit sit in the top third under pale haze. A giant rubber plug on a chain sits just offshore, and its chain snaps taut on frame 1 as the first swirl forms. A paper-cut vintage surfer (a public-domain Waikiki photo) rides a small wave near the shore. The yellow dashed SEA LEVEL line sits on the real 0 m contour, with a 'SEA LEVEL' plate (Barlow 800, cap 88 px) at x 80-480, y about 700.

Then the camera, low on the moat floor, tilts up one single mountain with the surfer a speck at its very top: "That surfer was riding the very tip of all this." Then the ocean roars back, and the plug drops into its hole on the last word.

seven.why:

Everyone who watches it is primed to recognise the long-form's card later in Suggested and Browse. It pays off the title ('only the tip') without spending the film's Everest beat or its 56,000-ft climax.

seven.concept:
WORKING TITLE: You Can't Walk From Maui to Lanai (Unless...). About 25 s, 51 words. The one big number is -400 FEET. Release on D+1.

Molokai's east end appears at the right edge only if the framing allows; Kaho'olawe stays out of frame. The paper tourist, in a red aloha shirt with a suitcase (a public-domain traveller photo; rights check), stands at the waterline centre-left with his feet at y about 1350. During the refill he grabs his suitcase and sprints back ahead of the rising water, while the ferry rights itself and floats. - 0.0-2.7: Hook.
- 2.7-5.8: VO: 'Unless we drain four hundred feet of ocean.' On 'drain', a gurgle and riser play and the water starts to fall. '-400' (Anton cap 260, yellow) with FEET (Barlow cap 96) rolls in at x 80-700, y 230-560.

seven.why:
Its payoff is the long-form's 0:14 hero shot. Anyone who taps through from this Short sees what they came for within 20 s of the film, which is the best first Related Video experience we can give.

The premise has real Shorts demand: inter-island travel pulls 5.4M, 181K and 77K, and lost land bridges pull 3.6M, 806K and 187K (Doggerland). Yet 'Maui Nui' has zero geology Shorts.

P2-02's hook beat S02's. It gives a character with a goal and an obstacle in 3 s, using a line everyone knows is true, instead of opening on a number. At 25 s it is the second-shortest Short. Something moves every 2 s, and the 'will he make it back?' chase resolves only on the loop line.

seven.concept:
WORKING TITLE: Where Did Half of This Volcano Go? About 33 s, 71 words. The one big number is 125 MILES. Release on D+3.

PREMISE: A tourist at Oahu's windy Nu'uanu Pali Lookout loses his hat. We follow it down the cliffs and out to sea, drain the ocean, and find the rest of the Ko'olau volcano lying on the sea floor in giant blocks. One block is bigger than Manhattan, and the hat lands on it. An updraft brings the hat home, and the idiom lands as the punchline.

A paper tourist (a public-domain photo of a man in a hat; rights check) stands at the railing in the lower-left third. Jagged green cliffs fill the frame behind him and cloud tatters race past. Kicker: PALI LOOKOUT, OAHU (Barlow 800 cap 80, y about 240). On frame 0 the hat is already lifting off his head, with a gust sound.

A crash zoom finds the tiny hat sitting on it. Then the scale snaps out along a trail of wreckage about 125 miles long, 'one of the largest landslides on Earth.' The final gag payoff: the hat lands back on his head.

LOOP: Read together: 'So if you ever stand at this railing, hold on to your hat, because / about half of this volcano is missing.' During the refill the hat floats up off the block. An updraft carries it back across the sea and up the cliffs, and the camera follows on an eased move into the opening pose. The hat drops onto his head, and that is frame 0, where the next gust lifts it again. The wind whoosh runs straight across the cut. Record VO8 and VO1 as one take.

- 0.0-2.7: The hat lifts and tumbles over the railing. VO1.
- 2.7-6.2: A 2 s eased dive chases the hat down the cliff face. VO: 'These cliffs on Oahu are where it broke off.' (VERIFY)
- 6.2-10.1: The hat flutters out over the windward sea and the camera rises to a regional oblique northeast of Oahu. VO: 'Long before anyone lived here, it slid into the sea.'
- 10.1-13.5: Drain to about -4,000 m. Blocks surface one by one under a low sun, with a thump about every second, and the depth gauge sits on the left edge. VO: 'Drain the ocean, and it's still lying there.'
- 13.5-17.0: The Manhattan slam (impact_deep sound, dust puff). A MANHATTAN plate lands (Barlow 800 cap 92, x 80-600, y 560-680). Crash zoom to the hat (a soft 'boop'). VO: 'One piece is bigger than Manhattan.'
- 17.0-23.5: A 3 s pull-back along the debris trail, which lights up in hero orange. Number block: ABOUT (Barlow cap 80), '125' (Anton cap 260, yellow), MILES (Barlow cap 96), at x 80-860, y 230-560. VO: 'The wreckage runs for about a hundred and twenty-five miles. One of the largest landslides on Earth.'
- 23.5-33.0: The refill, the hat's flight home, and its landing on frame 0. VO: 'So if you ever stand at this railing, hold on to your hat, because...' (cut at 33.0).

- (b) The block size. USGS words it 'about the same size as Manhattan Island', but the ODP Leg 200 site report gives the Tuscaloosa block as about 30 x 17 km. seven.why:
It is the only Short for Ch2, which starts at 1:20, so a viewer who taps through reaches it in under 90 s.

It has the strongest thread in the set. A physical gag is already moving in frame 0, and the hat then becomes the camera's guide. Viewers watch to see where it lands (on the Manhattan block) and whether he gets it back (the last word).

seven.concept:
WORKING TITLE: Hawaii's Big Island Will End Up Like This. About 34.5 s, 79 words. The one big number is 28 MILLION YEARS. Release on D+5.

PREMISE: Open on Midway's ring of coral and call it the Big Island's future. Then one eased flight northwest along the real chain shows a Hawaiian island's whole life: born on the hot spot, carried off the heat, sinking, carved into canyons, a sliver of rock people once farmed, one last tooth, and finally a ring of coral on a volcano that sank out of sight. That last stage is frame 0.

HOOK: VO at 0.0 s: 'Hawaii's Big Island will end up looking like this.' ('Big Island will end up' lands by 1.5 s.) Frame 0: Midway Atoll in true colour from a high vertical oblique. The white-and-turquoise reef ring fills about 70% of the frame height, set in deep blue water, with a 6 px white rim and a slow orbit already moving. For sound-off viewers, the headline THE BIG ISLAND'S FUTURE (Anton cap 110, 4 words) sits at x 80-880, y 230-360.

PAYOFF: Every stage is a real island at its real position; nothing morphs. The destination is the ring we opened on: 'Then just a ring of coral, on a volcano that sank out of sight. About twenty-eight million years old.' The number block 'ABOUT / 28 / MILLION YEARS' lands as the orbit picks up its opening path.

LOOP: Read together: 'Every island on this line takes the same trip. Which means / Hawaii's Big Island will end up looking like this.' The final eased move arrives on Midway in the exact opening pose and at the same orbit speed. The headline returns in the last 0.5 s, so the orbit simply continues across the cut. The ocean-swell ambience runs through it. Record VO10 and VO1 as one take.

BEATS:
- 0.0-3.5: Orbit on the ring. VO1.
- 3.5-5.0: A whip-pan of 6-8 frames with motion blur, southeast to the Big Island. It is huge, with lava glowing at the coast and a 55% orange fill.
- 5.0-11.0: A 3 s cut-away sliver shows the glowing plume and the plate sliding northwest 'like paper over a candle' (15 px arrow). A slim age bar along the top (y about 210, no digits) starts to fill. VO: 'A hot spot builds a giant volcano. Then the sea floor slides it northwest, off the heat.'
- 11.0-12.6: An eased 1.5 s move until Maui fills the frame. VO: 'It starts to sink.'
- 12.6-14.6: Kaua'i's canyons in raking light. VO: 'Rain carves it into canyons.'
- 14.6-18.5: Nihoa, a sliver of cliff in the swell, with terrace lines drawing on in yellow. VO: 'Then it's a sliver of rock that people once farmed.'
- 18.5-20.1: La Perouse Pinnacle with a yellow rim. VO: 'Then one last tooth.'
- 20.1-28.0: Back to the Midway ring on the orbit path. Number block: ABOUT (Barlow cap 80), '28' (Anton cap 300, yellow), MILLION YEARS (Barlow cap 100), at x 80-860, y 220-600. VO: 'Then just a ring of coral, on a volcano that sank out of sight. About twenty-eight million years old.'
- 28.0-34.5: The orbit eases into the opening pose and the age bar fades. VO: 'Every island on this line takes the same trip. Which means...' (cut at 34.5).
Each island fills at least a third of the frame. Every move takes 1.5-2.5 s and is eased. All text stays inside x 72-900, y 200-1500.

FACTS: Spine #8, #9, #10 and #11, plus #4 for the sinking. 'Will end up looking like this' is the film's own framing (at 9:55: 'So that's the Big Island's future'). VERIFY that the fact-check accepts it as the chain's pattern rather than a guarantee. Fallback hook: 'This is where Hawaii's Big Island is headed.'

REUSES: The Ch3 twist (5:15-5:45), the Ch4 hot-spot cut-away and candle metaphor (5:45-6:05), the TIME MACHINE flight over Maui and Kaua'i (6:05-7:00), the Nihoa terraces on the DEM (7:00), La Perouse (7:30), the Midway ring and its 28-million-year counter (8:00-8:45), and the GEBCO data for the northwest chain. New, Short only: the reversed order (the future comes first), the single vertical flight, and the loop that works by orbit continuity.
seven.why:
It is the long-form's backbone in 35 s: Ch3's twist, all of Ch4 and the start of Ch5. That makes it the Short that advertises the most minutes of the film.

The hidden-chain premise is the second most proven in the probe (14M, 7.4M, 2.3M), yet the life-cycle angle exists only as flat diagrams (16K, 14K, 10K, 1.3K). It has the cleanest loop of the seven, because the destination literally is the first frame, and a new shape arrives every 1.5-3 s.

S06 beat P2-06 because a bright ring is a far more arresting phone frame than open water, and 'Big Island' is concrete. Nihoa (S07) is folded in as one stage, with its human line.

Because this Short owns 'Midway is a ring of coral on a sunken volcano', the albatross and Darwin Shorts (S09, P2-09, P2-10) were cut: they pay off on the same reveal. The seal Shorts (S08, P2-05) were cut for the same reason, since French Frigate Shoals and its 'last rock' are a stage here.

seven.concept:
WORKING TITLE: The Carriers Sunk at Midway Aren't at Midway. About 30 s, 63 words. The one big number is 3 MILES DOWN. Solemn: no gags, music down, treated as war graves. Release on D+7.

PREMISE: A respectful myth-bust. The Battle of Midway is named after the atoll, but drain the Pacific and draw the line, and the three carriers found so far lie far out on the flat ocean floor, about three miles down. Two have never been found. The last line says why: the fleets fought with planes, from far out at sea.

HOOK: VO at 0.0 s: 'The carriers sunk at Midway aren't at Midway.' (3.1 s; 'carriers sunk at Midway' lands by 1.5 s.) Frame 0: a low golden-hour oblique from Midway's outer reef edge, looking northwest to the open sea. The reef and Sand Island sit in the lower foreground, above y 1500. This is deliberately not the top-down ring that #4 uses. A thick yellow line (12 px core, dark under-stroke, head dot) is already drawing from the reef toward the horizon. A MIDWAY plate (Barlow 800 cap 96) sits at x 80-460, y 240-340. A low drone bed plays, with no music sting.

PAYOFF: The camera follows the line's head dot out over the drained abyssal plain. Then it plunges straight down the frame, using the 9:16 frame as a depth gauge, to three simple home-built hull silhouettes, each in an inset zoom circle: 'Far out on the flat ocean floor, three have been found, about three miles down.' Then: 'Two have never been found.'

LOOP: Read together: 'The fleets fought with planes, from far out at sea. That's why / the carriers sunk at Midway aren't at Midway.' The refill rises, and the camera climbs the water column and flies back along the line. The line retracts to the reef edge as the camera settles into the opening pose, and frame 0 is the same pose with the line starting to draw out again. The drone bed runs across the cut. Record VO7 and VO1 as one take.

BEATS:
- 0.0-3.1: Hook.
- 3.1-9.4: The public-domain NHHC Yorktown photo, 2.5 s full-bleed with a slow push (VERIFY the credit), then back to the atoll as the drain starts. VO: 'In June 1942, four Japanese carriers and the USS Yorktown went down.'
- 9.4-13.7: The atoll stands up as a coral cap on a drowned volcano, and the camera follows the line out. VO: 'Drain the Pacific, and you'd find them nowhere near the island.'
- 13.7-16.4: The line runs 170-190 miles out. Its length shows the distance, so no number is spoken. VO: 'Far out on the flat ocean floor,'
- 16.4-19.6: The vertical plunge to the three silhouettes. Number block: ABOUT (Barlow cap 80), '3' (Anton cap 280, yellow), MILES DOWN (Barlow cap 96), at x 80-860, y 220-560. VO: 'three have been found, about three miles down.'
- 19.6-22.4: Two empty dashed hull outlines appear as an icon in the text area, not on the map, so no positions are implied. VO: 'Two have never been found.'
- 22.4-30.0: The refill and the return along the retracting line. VO: 'The fleets fought with planes, from far out at sea. That's why...' (cut at 30.0).
All text stays inside x 72-900, y 200-1500.

FACTS: Spine #14 (four Japanese carriers sunk, Yorktown lost). Spine #15: Kaga about 5.4 km down and about 190 mi out; Yorktown about 5 km down and about 172 mi out; Akagi found in 2019; Soryu and Hiryu unfound. Must-fix #2: only the three surveyed wrecks, our own hull silhouettes, never OET, NOAA or Vulcan imagery, and no treasure framing. VERIFY Akagi's depth and position (not in the spine) and the closing line 'the fleets fought with planes, from far out at sea' (standard history, but not in the spine). The decoy story was dropped: about 20 copycat Shorts on it flopped at 130-3,000 views, and its wording is still VERIFY.

REUSES: The Ch5 battle beat (8:45-9:30) and its NHHC Yorktown photo, the honest wreck line with the home-built hull silhouettes (9:30-9:55), and the Midway drain and reef cap (8:15). New, Short only: the reef-edge opening, the camera that follows the head dot, the vertical depth plunge and the line-retract loop.
seven.why:
It is the only Short that sells Ch5's 'battle over a drowned volcano', and it reaches the long-form's biggest adjacent audience: US WWII viewers. Midway Shorts pull 5.7M and 5.1M, 'The Carrier That Sank Twice' 1.5M, and Nat Geo's 'Pacific War Wrecks | Drain the Oceans' (2.47M, long-form) proves the drain-plus-wrecks idea.

The paradox hook is on-brand for Myth Juice and true as worded ('carriers', not 'ships'). The vertical plunge is the best use of the 9:16 frame in the set, and 'two have never been found' is a real open mystery that drives comments.

The merge: P2-07's depth plunge and its unfound-two beat went into S10's myth-bust frame, and S10's decoy beat was cut. This Short beat the seal and albatross Shorts because those would repeat #4's sunken-volcano reveal, while this one covers ground nothing else does.

seven.concept:
WORKING TITLE: The Most Optimistic Sign in Hawaii. About 25 s, 48 words. The one big number is 3,200 FEET. Release on D+8 or D+9.

PREMISE: A paper real-estate sign reading COMING SOON / NEW ISLAND sticks out of the open ocean off the Big Island. As the water drains, the camera rides its pole down, and down, and down, 3,200 ft to the summit of a young volcano that could become the next Hawaiian island. Opening date: thousands of years, at least.

HOOK: VO at 0.0 s: 'This is the most optimistic sign in Hawaii.' (3.1 s.) Frame 0: open ocean off the Big Island's southeast coast, with Kilauea's coastline and a steam plume on the horizon in the top third. In the centre, a paper sign on a pole bobs in the waves. The board reads COMING SOON (Anton cap 130) over NEW ISLAND (Anton cap 96), inside x 120-860, y 700-1100. Nothing else is in the frame.

PAYOFF: The pole that never ends is a comic hold that also delivers the number. It finally lands on the summit of a small dark cone (THUNK), and a pull-back shows the baby beside the giant massif. Then: 'Opening date? Thousands of years, at least.' An ISH sticker slaps onto the sign after SOON.

LOOP: Read together: '...Thousands of years, at least. Which means / this is the most optimistic sign in Hawaii.' The refill climbs the pole and the camera rides the waterline back up. A gust peels the ISH sticker away and the sign settles into the frame-0 bob phase: same horizon, same bob. The wave sound is continuous. Record VO8 and VO1 as one take.

- 0.0-3.1: Hook.
- 3.1-4.3: VO: 'Follow the pole.' The drain starts with a gurgle, and the camera tilts down and rides the pole below the falling waterline.
- 4.3-9.5: VO: 'Three thousand two hundred feet down,' '3,200' (Anton cap 260, yellow) with FEET (Barlow cap 96) rolls in at x 80-860, y 230-520 while the pole keeps going (a comic hold with a pole creak).
- 9.5-13.0: VO: 'it stands on the summit of a young volcano.' The pole ends, planted in the cone (THUNK).
- 13.0-15.5: An eased 2 s pull-back shows the cone on the Big Island's drained flank, with the massif towering above. Optional caption plate KAMA'EHUAKANALOA (Barlow 800 cap 84, x 80-900, y 600-720), never spoken. VO: 'A baby, next to the giants.'
- 15.5-18.5: VO: 'It could become the next Hawaiian island.'
- 18.5-22.0: VO: 'Opening date?' (beat) 'Thousands of years, at least.' The ISH sticker slaps on with 'least'.
- 22.0-25.5: The refill rises up the pole, the sticker blows off, and the shot returns to frame 0. VO: 'Which means...' (cut at 25.5).
All text stays inside x 72-900, y 200-1500.

FACTS: Spine #16: the summit is 975 m (3,200 ft) below sea level, it 'could' become the next island, and it will take 'thousands of years at least'. The narration never says 'erupting' or 'active'. The island claim lives only on our joke sign and is hedged by the VO's 'could'. The name is a caption only, so the voice cannot mangle it.

REUSES: The Ch6 opener (10:15-10:45): the young cone on the drained south flank 3,200 ft down, and the COMING SOON sign gag with 'thousands of years at least'. New, Short only: the sign starts above the water on an absurdly long pole, so the vertical drain becomes a measuring tape; the ISH sticker (from S11); and the bob loop.
seven.why:
It is the only Short for Ch6's newborn-volcano beat and the shortest of the seven. It works as a light palate cleanser between the solemn wrecks Short and the big finale.

The frame-0 image, a sign in the open ocean, asks 'on what?' without any words, and the pole that never ends turns the one number into the joke. The premise is unclaimed (Hawaii-specific versions sit at 2.3K and 4.1K), while island-birth Shorts pull 2.2M and 95K.

P2-08's pole structure beat S11's refill-then-drain-again, which is confusing, and S11's 'already under construction' hook stated the island as certain. S11's ISH sticker was kept as the punchline. The new hook keeps every factual claim under the VO's 'could'.

S05 and P2-04 (the Everest parking gag) lost their place because 'taller than Everest' is spent, and #7 already uses Everest as a stepping stone.

seven.concept:
WORKING TITLE: This Beach Is on a Mountain Almost Twice Everest. About 35 s, 73 words. The one big number is 56,000 FEET. Publish no earlier than D+7 (planned for D+10), with the long-form as its Related Video.

PREMISE: One vertical crane shot travels from a black-sand beach on Mauna Loa's lava down through the draining ocean, past the sea floor, and into the dent the mountain's weight has pressed into the planet. Then it rises back up the whole height while the counter climbs to about 56,000 ft, and Everest, on the same base line, reaches about halfway. It is deliberately the opposite of #1: the southwest side (Mauna Loa) instead of the northeast, a fast drain and a cut-away instead of a slow countdown, and a height claim instead of 'the tip'.

HOOK: VO at 0.0 s: 'This beach is on a mountain almost twice as tall as Everest.' (4.7 s; 'beach is on a mountain' lands by 1.6 s.) Frame 0: a low vertical oblique on a black-sand beach on Mauna Loa's lava. A paper Hawaiian green sea turtle (a public-domain NOAA or USFWS photo) basks in the lower third and surf rolls in. Mauna Loa's broad summit sits at the top under pale haze. The headline ALMOST TWICE EVEREST (Anton cap 120) sits at x 80-880, y 230-380. The crane is already easing downward.

PAYOFF: Everest sinks to the dent's base line, and the camera cranes up the full height while 'ABOUT / 56,000 / FEET' rolls. Everest reaches about halfway: 'Measured from its real base, Mauna Loa is about fifty-six thousand feet tall.'

LOOP: Read together: 'And that turtle has no idea / this beach is on a mountain almost twice as tall as Everest.' The crane continues up through the refilling ocean and decelerates to a stop in the opening beach pose, and the headline returns. This is a natural hang at zero speed: frame 0 is the same pose with the crane easing down from rest. The surf sound bridges the cut. Record VO8 and VO1 as one take.

BEATS:
- 0.0-4.7: Hook.
- 4.7-8.6: The camera dips below the waterline as the ocean drains in one fast 2 s whoosh. There is no countdown, so it never repeats #1. A MAUNA LOA plate lands (Barlow 800 cap 92, x 80-560, y 600-720). VO: 'Drain the ocean, and most of Mauna Loa was underwater.' (VERIFY)
- 8.6-11.8: The camera reaches the sea floor. Everest (the SRTM mesh on a pedestal that starts from the same base, VE 1.0) rises beside it, just short. VO: 'From the sea floor, it already beats Everest.' (VERIFY)
- 11.8-13.8: The camera keeps going and the ground slices open. VO: 'But that's not the bottom.'
- 13.8-21.5: The crust and Moho sag into a bowl (schematic, drawn from the USGS flexure description), with a 3 s inset of a paper bowling ball pressing into a mattress. VO: 'It's so heavy, it has pushed the ocean floor down, by miles. Like a bowling ball on a mattress.'
- 21.5-28.5: Everest sinks to the dent's base line and the crane climbs the whole height. Number block: ABOUT (Barlow cap 80), '56,000' (Anton cap 240, yellow), FEET (Barlow cap 96), at x 80-860, y 220-540. An EVEREST label (Barlow cap 92) sits at its summit. VO: 'Measured from its real base, Mauna Loa is about fifty-six thousand feet tall.'
- 28.5-35.0: The crane rises through the refilling ocean to the beach. VO: 'And that turtle has no idea...' (cut at 35.0).
VE is 1.0 throughout. All text stays inside x 72-900, y 200-1500.

FACTS: Spine #2: about 56,000 ft from its true base, the sea floor pushed down by as much as 5 miles, always named Mauna Loa, always 'almost twice'. Spine #3: Everest is 29,032 ft. VERIFY in the USGS 'How high is Mauna Loa?' article behind #2 that more of Mauna Loa lies below sea level than above, and that from the sea floor alone it already tops Everest. Fallback: cut VO3 and hold the Everest pop-up silent. VERIFY that the chosen beach is on Mauna Loa lava (USGS geologic map). Punalu'u is the famous turtle beach, but which volcano's flank it sits on must be confirmed; otherwise use a Ka'u or South Kona beach on Mauna Loa. The turtle is optional; the fallback is S12's sunbather.

REUSES: The Ch3 Everest side-by-side at VE 1.0 (3:55-4:30), the Mauna Loa highlight (4:40-5:15), the Ch6 payoff cut-away with the crust and Moho sag, the bowling-ball metaphor, the 56,000 counter and Everest sunk to the same base (11:10-11:45), and the refill (11:45-12:30). New, Short only: one continuous vertical crane down and back up, the turtle beach on Mauna Loa, and the paper bowling-ball inset.
seven.why:
It is the strongest premise of the 24. It carries the most proven idea on Shorts ('Everest is not the tallest': 17M, 2.1M, 421K) with a number nobody uses (the closest Short to 56,000 ft has 263 views). But it spends the long-form's climax, so it goes last: after the film's first week, to re-ignite it in week 2.

It turns the spent fact into a stepping stone ('it already beats Everest... but that's not the bottom'). That is why it beat S05 and P2-04, which end on the spent fact.

S12 beat P2-01 because 'every photo is cropped' is the same 'only the tip' premise as #1, while 'almost twice Everest' is a distinct, testable height claim. P2-01's 'the sea floor isn't the bottom' beat lives on as VO4.

The 9:16 frame suits one continuous crane down and up, and the turtle keeps the cast distinct from #1's surfer, so the two Big Island Shorts share neither a premise, a device, a side of the island nor a payoff.
